text: 三个臭皮匠，顶个诸葛亮
pinyin: sān gè chòu pí jiàng, dǐng gè zhū gě liàng
literal: three · (measure word) · smelly · cobbler, equal · (measure word) · Zhuge Liang
natural: Three smelly cobblers are a match for one Zhuge Liang

meaning.en: Ordinary people pooling their ideas can match a genius.
meaning.zh: 比喻人多智慧多，几个普通人的智慧合起来，能顶一个聪明人。

equivalents: two heads are better than one

examples.zh: 这个问题我们一起讨论吧，三个臭皮匠，顶个诸葛亮。
examples.en: Let's work through this problem together — two heads are better than one.

story.en: Zhuge Liang (181–234), chancellor of Shu Han in the Three Kingdoms period, is the archetype of wisdom in Chinese culture. A popular theory holds that 皮匠 "cobbler" was originally 裨将 pí jiàng "deputy general" — three deputy generals together could match Zhuge Liang — and the words merged in speech because they sound alike.
story.zh: 诸葛亮是三国时期蜀汉丞相，在中国文化中是智慧的化身。有一种说法认为"皮匠"原是"裨将"（副将），意思是三个副将的智慧合起来能比得上诸葛亮，后来因为读音相近而讹传为"皮匠"。

usage.en: Said to encourage teamwork and brainstorming. Humorous and modest (you call your own group "smelly cobblers"). Also 三个臭皮匠，赛过诸葛亮.
usage.zh: 多用于鼓励集思广益，带有自谦和幽默色彩。也说"三个臭皮匠，赛过诸葛亮"。

synonyms: 一个篱笆三个桩，一个好汉三个帮

pinyin: chī yī qiàn, zhǎng yī zhì
literal: eat · one · pit, grow · one · wisdom
natural: Fall into a pit once and you grow a little wiser

meaning.en: Every setback makes you wiser; you learn from your mistakes.
meaning.zh: 受一次挫折，便长一分见识。

examples.zh: 上次因为没备份丢了论文，吃一堑，长一智，现在我每天都备份文件。
examples.en: Last time I lost my essay because I hadn't backed it up. Lesson learned — now I back up my files every day.

story.en: The idea goes back to a letter by the Ming philosopher Wang Shouren (Wang Yangming): "Whoever stumbles once gains a bit of wisdom; today's loss may well become tomorrow's gain." The rhyming spoken form 吃一堑，长一智 later became the usual version.
story.zh: 明代思想家王守仁（王阳明）在给薛尚谦的信中写道："经一蹶者长一智，今日之失，未必不为后日之得。"后来民间说成"吃一堑，长一智"。

usage.en: Used after a mistake, to sum up the lesson or to comfort someone. 堑 qiàn ("moat, pit") is rare outside this saying; 长 is read zhǎng ("grow"), not cháng.
usage.zh: 多用于犯错之后总结教训或安慰别人。"堑"读 qiàn，"长"读 zhǎng。

pinyin: bǎi wén bù rú yī jiàn
literal: hundred · hear · not · as good as · one · see
natural: Hearing something a hundred times is not as good as seeing it once

meaning.en: Seeing something for yourself beats hearing about it many times.
meaning.zh: 听别人说一百次，不如亲眼看一次。指亲眼看到的比听来的更可靠。

examples.zh: 大家都说桂林山水美，这次亲自去了才知道，真是百闻不如一见。
examples.en: Everyone says Guilin's scenery is beautiful, but only after going myself did I really understand — seeing is believing.

story.en: When the Qiang people rose up in the northwest, Emperor Xuan of Han asked the general Zhao Chongguo, then over seventy, how many troops would be needed. Zhao replied: "Hearing a hundred times is not as good as seeing once. It is hard to plan a campaign from afar — let me ride to Jincheng and draw up a plan there." He studied the terrain in person and proposed stationing soldiers to farm the frontier, which eventually brought peace to the region.
story.zh: 汉宣帝时，西北羌人叛乱。汉宣帝问七十多岁的老将赵充国需要派多少兵马，赵充国说："百闻不如一见。兵难遥度，臣愿驰至金城，图上方略。"他亲自到前线察看地形，提出屯田戍边的策略，最终平定了叛乱。

usage.en: Said when something seen in person turns out better than (or different from) what you'd heard. Common in travel talk. Sometimes extended: 百闻不如一见，百见不如一干 ("seeing beats hearing; doing beats seeing").
usage.zh: 常用于亲眼见到之后发出感叹，谈旅游时尤其常用。有人扩展为"百闻不如一见，百见不如一干"。
